utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. You may begin. Let us have the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. The witness is Mirko Babik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Babik, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I shall be going through a few of the first questions fairly rapidly to save time. From your CV I see that after secondary school, you were enrolled at the faculty of medicine in Skopje. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you -- for some private reasons, you interrupted your studies in your last year, so you didn't actually graduate although you got to the last stage. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From 1973, or more precisely, from January 1973, you have been working in the emergency service in Skopje as a medical technician; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means for over 30 years. Have you been working continuously during those 30 years?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, continuously in that service for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your capacity there, did you work there during the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did work there in that capacity during the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the bombing, were you -- did you do a medical duty work in the border belt towards the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the border belt from the very beginning. We did shifts at Donje Blace and later on Stenkovac 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "from the very beginning," was this regular duty work immediately after the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. Our shifts and duty work was after that. Not at the beginning, not for the first few days, but from the 1st of April, we had round the clock, 24 hour stints or shifts, permanent shifts there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you would take regular shifts very frequently?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. We had a rapid succession of shifts, and we would go to do our stints very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? Can you explain that to us? How do you mean "frequently"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Well, we had shifts in town in our basic workplace, and we had to go out in the field. We had three teams on duty, which meant that the three teams replaced one another fairly frequently, on a fairly regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say, you were at the approach to Donje Blace, which is across from the Djeneral Jankovic crossing; is that right? Border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you start doing duty work in the holding camps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: I started working in the holding camps sometime around the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just establish the exact time, because the previous two witnesses spoke about this same situation. Tell us when those holding camps were established first, from the border crossing. When were the refugees accommodated in the camps? According to my information, that would be between the 5th and 6th of April. Is that correct or did that happen earlier?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Stenkovac was established sometime around the 5th and 6th of April. That is when they were transferred to Stenkovac 1, and then later on to Stenkovac 2. That means the 5th or 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's get right to the point now in medias res. Throughout that time did you happen to notice or, rather, you took in patients. You saw patients; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, did you come across a single Albanian coming in from Kosovo who had perhaps been beaten or had suffered from any side, let's say the police, the army, or anybody else? Did you notice anybody like that who had come in beaten up?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice any Albanian who had been beaten up or beaten by the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to notice that anybody had been beaten by anybody else? I mean, did you see any injuries consistent with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take in patients regularly, see patients regularly in your capacity as medical technician whose job it is to see patients?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I saw them regularly, and I was the first person to come into contact with a patient, actually. I received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And throughout that time, did you come across any Albanian who was wounded, either by firearms or by a knife or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any entrance/exit wounds or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did anybody come to contact you and complain that he had been beaten by the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: On one occasion one Albanian did come to me. He was standing in front of our makeshift clinic and said he had been beaten up and that he was all black and blue. He said he was black and blue, like liver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "dzigarica," that word means "liver" in Serbian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. He was black and blue, but looking at his hands and face and the areas that I could see and the way he moved around and walked, I wasn't able to establish anything like that. And then I said, "Well, you can come into our field examination room and we'll examine you." He changed the subject straight away and asked me how far it was to Skopje. I said it was about 23 kilometres away. And in the meantime, another man and woman came into the examination room. I told them to take a seat, and the man got lost. He just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you offered to examine him, and he just disappeared, left the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. I said that we would help him and take a look at him, examine him, but he just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him to show you the bruises that he talked about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him to come into the infirmary to -- for me to take a look, to examine him, but he just got lost and disappeared very soon after that. I can also say that there was another Albanian who came to see me, a man of about 70 years of age, and he said that he lived in a village and that he had some livestock and several milking cows, and he said that some people had come and told him to leave his house. He didn't want to. He said he was an old man and didn't want to go up into the fields and hills and live with his cattle. One of the men had a firearm, and with that firearm he shot a round of bullets in the direction of the roof of the house and said that if they find him there next time they come round, they'd kill him, and they would blow the house up. And they went off in a direction that was known to him. There was a group of people. And he said, "This is where I turned up -- ended up." I asked him, which people were they? What language were they speaking? He looked to his left and to his right, and in an angry way he energetically pointed to the direction of the tent and the camp and pointed to his own people, in fact. And I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just get one thing straight here. Was that an example that the KLA was forcing civilians to join the refugees and go to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that they were -- or, rather, let me see that they -- he meant that they were his men and that that's what they wanted him to do, to move towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And another example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear from Mr. Babik. What exactly did your work as a medical technician involve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my duty was to administer therapy together with the doctor and to administer first aid. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means giving injections, bandaging wounds. I assume that if somebody needs a wound bandaged, you'd do that and not the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. First aid, that's what we were trained to do, and also therapy, drips, anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you got any other example?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Well, I also remember the story of a Roma, a man who came when the morning shift was on duty. He came in very much afraid and said he hadn't been able to have water or food for two days and the children were crying. And when we asked why they weren't being given food and water, a group of young men came in and beat them up. He managed to jump over the fence, he said, and same to see me, and ten metres away from us there was the police and the Red Cross. I went over there, and the man repeated the same story, and a policeman and a lady from the Red Cross went to see what all this was about, see what was going on in the tent. When they returned, I asked them what had happened. They said it was true, and then I saw them take the food to the people ten minutes later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly slow down for the benefit of the interpreters and the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Babik, the interpreter is asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babik, you were saying that the Albanians, in actual fact, as far as I was able to understand, mistreated the Roma in the refugee camp. They didn't allow them to get food, get to the food and the water and that the Macedonian policemen had to separate them from them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. The police had intervene, and afterwards they were transferred to another place, but that didn't help much either. And then they were transferred to some other camps; Cicino Selo, Selo Saraj near Skopje, and Momo Advodno [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you received the patients, I assume that you wrote down the entries -- wrote down the names of the people that came to see you and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. took their data. Did you do that or did somebody else do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: I did that, and so did the nurse. We kept our records regularly. And in the registers, if you look at them, there might be some misunderstanding, because very often --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether you kept the register and you wrote in the entries. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: In some of the columns we can see that there -- you have the name and surname recorded and some basic data, and then we would see an empty column, no diagnosis and no therapy. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do have an explanation. That would happen because the people would come in to be examined, there would be a crowd, and when we asked them to come in for an examination, they would just disappear. So that is why we would have the name and surname recorded when they first came to us, and then they would disappear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then they would disappear and you didn't have anything to fill in.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and then there would be an empty space in those two columns for the diagnosis and the therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First, let us establish how often you were on duty working with the refugees, be it at the border crossing where you received them or in the camps. How often did you do those stints?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Very often. Once in two or three days perhaps. And the same goes for my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that period, you had opportunity to meet a large number of patients, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Their complaints, their conditions, how would you characterise them? How would you categorise them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Since it was cold, they suffered from colds, laryngitis, respiratory problems. Also digestion problems because the food was dry mostly. There were some skin conditions because of lack of hygiene. There were many pregnant women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At border crossings and in camps, did you notice the presence of a large number of TV crews and reporters?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. They turned out in force. I will give you an example. On a morning shift, once we were sitting in our vehicle when a group of about 10 young men came behind our vehicle and almost stole our stretcher. I ran out of the car and said, "What's the matter? Do you need the stretcher? Shall I help you?" They said, "No, no. We'll bring the patient ourselves." And then they ran into the depth of the camp about 20 or 30 metres, and then I saw them put a young man on the stretcher. They put a young man on the stretcher. The young man was all crumpled, convulsive, like in great pain, while some cameramen were filming them. And when this scene was over, the young man got up from the stretcher, they cheerfully waved good-bye to each other, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was a staged scene, it's quite clear, isn't it? Did you see anything else that would be similar to that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes. On another occasion, I must say there was an elevation near our infirmary, they gathered a group of women, very old men, disabled people, and I saw them with my own eyes taking children, children of about 2 to 5 years of age, away from their mothers, and they gave the children to the old people as if those were their grandchildren, and then they would film them. When the first shots, the first recordings were over, they would change the order. The people from the back would be put in the front and vice versa, and then they filmed some more. And I saw this myself. I have no doubt about it. The people who were around, including myself, we reacted and we said, "Look what -- look at what they're doing." We summoned the police and the police chased them away. The most active in this staging game, in this rigging game, were the camera crews of the CNN and BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that when you take such small children away from their mothers and give them to some elderly men, the children naturally cry.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: The children weren't crying; they were wailing, screaming. The cameramen instructed the old men to take their tissues out of their pockets and wipe their eyes and pretend to be crying themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You witnessed this scene. What do you think was the purpose of this whole exercise?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: You don't have to be very clever to understand that the whole purpose of this was to -- to mediatise the suffering of the people, to make it seem even worse than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to Albanians from Kosovo, did they ever tell you why they left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: At the beginning, they were saying that they were fleeing bombs. I think it was a natural reaction. Later on, they started saying that the army and the police were chasing and beating them and that's why they were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did they change the story?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: As soon as they were moved to the Stenkovac 1 and 2 refugee camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they changed their account when they were transferred to the camps. When they came to the border, they still said they were running from the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you never saw anyone who was obviously beaten or injured?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: No, in all the time I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a woman who was a rape victim in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Close to us there was an Israeli hospital. They were the best equipped. We often came to see that hospital. They had a lot of gynaecologists, internists, et cetera, but they left not long after. And the morning -- one morning I came and found that the Israeli hospital had disappeared, and I asked the policeman, "What's this?" And he told me that they left because there was a rape attempt against an Israeli woman doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Nice, assist me in this matter. Where does the indictment allege that the refugees were maltreated? Is it in Kosovo or in Macedonia? Because this evidence that is being led, as I understand it, relates to the camps in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The allegation is -- what you say is right, Mr. Robinson, but this so-called indictment alleges that those same refugees ran to Macedonia after being shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "So-called indictment." The accused has got to remember the decorum with which he has to approach this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite so, Mr. Milosevic. We've been through that before. Totally inappropriate language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it is a mild word for the lies contained in what Mr. Nice calls the indictment. Mr. Robinson, it is alleged that hundreds of thousands of people were chased away from Kosovo by being shot at, by being beaten, and you read that in the report of the so-called humanitarian organisations, by gunfire, by beatings. And later on in Macedonia, among a crowd of refugees, there is not a single gunshot wound, there's not a single person bearing any marks of beatings. And it is clear that this is a media story launched first by Madeleine Albright to the effect that Serbs were expelling Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo. That story was launched first by the CNN and repeated here by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to clarify the allegations in the indictment. Your case would then be, Mr. Milosevic, that if the indictment does allege - and I'll ask Mr. Nice to clarify this - that these incidents of maltreatment took place in Kosovo, the mere fact that this evidence relates to Macedonia, to camps in Macedonia, would not make the evidence irrelevant, because if you have evidence in the camp in Macedonia that they arrived there without any signs of having been beaten and so on, then the inference is that they were not beaten in Kosovo. But let me just -- Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reference is, as I think volunteered yesterday, can be found at paragraph 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 59. I have that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that, of course, says nothing about maltreatment of refugees after they've left Kosovo. It says: "Some of these internally displaced persons remained inside of the province of Kosovo throughout the time period relevant to this indictment and many --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is a reference to inadequate medical --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- many persons died as a consequence of the harsh weather conditions, insufficient food, inadequate medical attention and exhaustion. Others eventually crossed over the Kosovo border into Albania, Macedonia and Montenegro or crossed the provincial boundary between Kosovo and Serbia." There is no allegation here about the treatment of these refugees in Macedonia, nor could there be. The accused, whatever his original purpose of leading this evidence, has focused yesterday and today on the significance for his case generally of the condition of these refugees as they were found in Macedonia, and it's on that basis that I'm going to approach the evidence and cross-examine on it to the very limited extent that I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Babik --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Babik, can I ask you one question for clarification. After the 5th of April, did you continue to work at the border crossing or was your work confined to the camps at Stenkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 5th and the 6th of April I worked in Stenkovac 1 and Stenkovac 2 refugee camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in paragraph 55, it says: "Forces of the FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner, forcibly expelled -- forcibly expelled thousands of -- hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians ... the forces of the FRY and Serbia intentionally created an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force," et cetera. Acts of brutality and violence. So if acts of brutality and violence have to be visible once these refugees crossed the border the next day, they must be evident to the medical staff who deals with them if they were so brutally treated. I can go on reading this indictment in many other sections, but the same thesis permeates the whole text, that the police and army troops beat people with rifle butts, with truncheons, et cetera. None of that happened, and that story doesn't hold water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 57, Mr. Nice, the middle, it says: "Kosovo Albanians were frequently intimidated --" this is the next line. "Many Kosovo Albanians --" let me just see. Judge Kwon was just showing me a paragraph that's relevant. Yes, it says: "Kosovo Albanians were frequently intimidated, assaulted or killed in public view to enforce the departure of their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. families and neighbours." Well, it depends on the form that the force took, but I'm not saying the evidence is not relevant. I was trying to determine to what paragraph it relates. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for Mr. Babik. I think that suffices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I observed yesterday --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I observed yesterday, the 65 ter summaries said nothing about the staging of events by television companies. I haven't yet been able to elicit a response from CNN. I will be playing a short clip in a second to the witness made by CNN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm curious to know, Mr. Nice, if the witness can indicate a reason for this taking place, because it's very difficult to work out why this would be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like to ask him or shall I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please. I'd be grateful if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things, Mr. Babik. Is it Babic or Babik, your name? Babic or Babik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Babik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I only ask because of the way it's turning up on the transcript. Now, you mentioned the BBC as being one of the two riggers of scenes. Can you name any BBC reporter who you can remember engaged in rigging of scenes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: I don't know any names, but I claim with full responsibility that this indeed happened. It happened ten metres away from our tent, the tent in which we were located, but I don't know any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question identified by His Honour Judge Bonomy is this: Can -- what reason was there, as far as you could judge it, for their rigging the evidence or rigging the content of their reports?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: I think they wanted to sensationalise the media picture about the suffering of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at a short clip which is one from CNN in light of something that your colleague mentioned yesterday, but we'll just look at it and see if you can help us with it. It's a CNN clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Forced from their homes, some of them say at gunpoint, suddenly the weather became their worst enemy. Standing shoulder to shoulder in a chilly rain, sickness set up. The oldest and the youngest, the most vulnerable targets. Throughout the day about every five minutes another extremely ill Kosovar refugee was hauled uphill from this mountain valley camp along the Yugoslav-Macedonian frontier. Doctors say 11 had died Friday night, and Saturday they feared the toll would rise even higher. "What's going to happen within a couple of days, if it's still raining like it is now and the people are still there? You can think of the diseases that are going to spread all over the place. No good. "The mountain climate along the frontier has been both a blessing and a curse. Refugees are suffering from exposure and upper respiratory problems but the cold climate has stopped the spread of infectious diseases like cholera. "Despair was another enemy. Kosovar Albanians who just a day or two ago had a roof over their heads now have only plastic. The healthy barely noticed as the sick passed them by. Life had been reduced to a struggle to stay warm, dry, and fed "They're living in mud. They're wet, they're dirty, they're tired, they're angry. They want to move on. They want to move to families, they want to go back home. "During the refugee rebellion, Macedonia brought in more soldiers and police to keep order. But a bureaucratic bottleneck worsened the situation. Thousands still waited in line to be registered, and despite an instant and growing refugee city of about 65.000, fewer have been evacuated by bus than the day before. The problem was so bad that Macedonia once again closed its border with Yugoslavia. "We are sitting here, women and children in the rain, said one very ill refugee. We are going to die. Escape from Kosovo for her, her husband, and thousands of other Kosovar Albanians have led nowhere but here. "Mike Betcher, CNN, on the Yugoslav-Macedonian border."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Babik --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it translated to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are not to speak when a Judge is speaking. That's just very basic protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just asked whether it was translated to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll check with the witness, shall I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Babik, as well as seeing what we were looking at, could you hear in your language a translation of what was being said by the newscaster?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: I'm afraid not. It wasn't interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that's the position, Your Honour, and I don't, I'm afraid, have time to -- well, if necessary I'll of course take some time to go back, but I know how limited my time is if I'm to stick within two-thirds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Mr. Milosevic wanted to say something. I don't know whether it's the same point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to draw your attention to the fact that the videotape wasn't interpreted, one; and second, certain things are said here that are contrary to what the witnesses were saying. One of them is that eight persons had died overnight in that camp. The witness should know about it because he worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the tape was not translated, Mr. Nice, we will not be able to rely on it unless we do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can rely on it simply for the visual images because those are all I want to ask about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Babik, it's this: We saw, according to the script on the screen, that part of that was Blace camp. Is that correct? And does that accord with your recollection of what Blace camp looked like?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: I only recognised a part of the area around Blace, around by the river Lepenac. The other infirmary, the Red Cross infirmary, I don't remember anything like that having been there. The other parts I can't recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The general picture of the condition of the camp and of the refugees as shown in that footage accurate? Was it accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: In those first few days when they started coming in, there was a little space and a lot of people, and they had lost their nearest and dearest along the way somewhere, so there were crowds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were hundreds of thousands of people in these camps eventually, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: In Stenkovac 1 and 2, yes, there were a lot of people. I don't know the exact number, but there were lots of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We also saw in the footage the presence of police and/or Macedonian army personnel. Is it right that such people were present in the camp at all times?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: The police was present, and as far as I remember, throughout the whole time, from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke of the difference in accounts given by individuals from the time when they were in the border camp until the time when they were moved to Stenkovac 1 and 2. At the border camp, in the first few days there were police and military present, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although we haven't focused on this, and it's not an issue that need necessarily trouble the Trial Chamber, the truth is that in the same way as there is tension between Albanians and Serbs, there is tension between Albanians and Macedonians; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Macedonia is the country that accepted the Albanian people, gave them assistance, and later on gave more than it was economically capable of extending. And even today it is helping the Romas who have stayed on in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In order to be brief if Mr. Prendergast would help me with page 113 of the "Under Orders" book, which is Exhibit 145. This summary is given by those who prepared this book. It says this of the exit to Macedonia: "There can be little doubt that the arrival of some 260.000 refugees from Kosovo placed an enormous strain on relations between ethnic Macedonians and ethnic Albanians in Macedonia. The government's go-slow policy in admitting refugees during the spring of 1999, the occasional police violence against the refugees, and the government's periodic refusal to admit --" just down a bit. "-- to admit additional refugees created enormous --" and then over the page, please, to finish this paragraph, five lines "-- created enormous resentment and anger among Macedonia's Albanians. Equally, the common cause shown by Macedonian Albanians for their Albanian neighbours from Kosovo fuelled fears about succession among ethnic Macedonians. The restraint shown by the leadership of the Albanian party in the ruling coalition, the Albanian Democratic Party, as well as the NATO presence, certainly helped prevent open conflict in Macedonia ..." Now, I only read that for completeness. My question to you is this: At the border crossing itself, is the truth that there was tension between Macedonians and Albanians because Albanians were anxious that they weren't going to be allowed in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Well, there shouldn't have been any fear because the Macedonians accepted those people and offered them selfless help and assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The border camp, which is a sort of holding camp against a background of a go-slow by the government and a stop-start of letting people in, there would be anxiety that people would be allowed to stay. Did you experience that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: We did our job. As to the rest, I'm not really informed enough about it to be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, you've given us various accounts of people talking to you about this and that. I take it that none of the people you spoke to is somebody you could identify so that I can go and speak to that person; correct? You can't identify any of the people you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: Well, that was in passing. I don't know what happened to those people later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could I just interrupt for a moment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Babik, you told us that people gave different reasons for being there; either because they were escaping from bombing or because they were claiming to have been attacked by Serb police or forces. Where did these people want to go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning, they said they just wanted to be safe and take refuge from the bombs, but later on they asked to go to third countries, to Europe, just transit through Macedonia on to other places. But many also asked to come to Macedonia to stay with their relatives and friends they had there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, if you're right, you and your two colleagues about the first account being accounts of people wanting to avoid the bombs and they subsequently giving an account of being forced out, I'm just going to suggest this to you: The first account may have been conditioned by the fact that they were facing Macedonian soldiers and police in the first interim camp at a time when they had no certainty they were going to be accepted. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: The Albanians knew that they would be taken in, accepted. We took them in, and the police and the army and all the services, the Red Cross, they saw that we were trying to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take it any further than that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the want of time, perhaps I can just say this: The -- I'm not going to ask the witness about it. The details of the numbers moved are contained in various reports. We can find the numbers moved into Macedonia and when. Neill Wright, from UNHCR. It's in "As Seen, As Told." The figures are all there. Perhaps I should deal with this once with one witness so that at least I've put it. If you'd like, please, to look at "As Seen, As Told," page 99. Just one piece of evidence that we have which suggests that the flow of refugees to Macedonia started - and these are cumulative figures - was 16.000 as at about the 23rd of March; 20.500 as at about the 30th; 28.000 as about the 31st; and then sharply rising on the 1st of April through the 3rd of April. So those are just figures by an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of those figures, Mr. Babik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: I don't know the figures. I can't confirm or otherwise refute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just take a look at the column here where it says the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. If you add up those figures, you would get almost 1.5 million. So these are unbelievable figures. Just look at the days. 116.000 every day from the 3rd of April to the 14th of April. Every day, there are over 100.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's plainly a running total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice and Mr. Milosevic, I'm keen to discover the reason for the change in attitude of the refugees, but I'd like to ascertain it on the basis of evidence, not speculation. So I certainly don't want Mr. Milosevic to comment on it, but of course he may address us on it in his final address. But if we could get evidence that would explain the difference, why this change in explanation from fleeing bombs to fleeing Serb persecution and violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my position is as follows, and it may help the accused despite -- especially in light of some of the observations he makes, to understand that this is the way is these courts operate. I can raise responsibilities where they seem reasonable, and I then raise them as possibilities. I can make assertions or direct propositions where I have good reason to make those assertions. So if one takes the previous witness -- not the previous witness, the witness who took rather longer, three witnesses ago, who produced a great deal of material that identified people, when we'd spoken to those people, one in particular, we found that there was a very clear reason for saying something that didn't accord with that person's experience; namely, he was frightened of the presence of figures of authority standing behind the interpreter. He had a reason to give the account. I was then in a position to advance that as the explanation for what was coming, apparently, from that video tape. Now, with these last three witnesses, no detail of any kind has been provided that will enable me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the videotape, you couldn't see any armed people standing around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Nice is on his feet. When Mr. Nice is finished, then you can raise your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'll have to be sure that I can pick up the train of my thought otherwise, as it was once said, I'll have to go right back to the beginning, but I've got a transcript to help me. With these witnesses, no detail of any kind has been provided that will enable me to send someone to speak to them to find out first whether the witnesses are telling the truth; and second, if they are, what was the explanation for the reason given. And it looks as though I'm never going to be provided with the identification or identity of any such person to whom I can go and speak, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think we have heard that. You must deal with it -- you have to deal with the case as you get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But Your Honour asked me the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know, I just made the observation. I just made the observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I said I don't want a comment from Mr. Milosevic, and I don't want a comment from you either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I am commenting because I'm trying to explain the position so that the accused can understand it. In those circumstances, I'm exploring a possibility with this witness, which is the explanation I've raised with him, and at the moment I can go no further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks. Mr. Milosevic, what's the objection that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice explained how on the videotape you could see the existence of armed people there, which is incorrect. You can't see that on the tape. And I should like to remind you of this: Even that chef de cabinet, Rugovin Rugovci [phoen], when I showed him his own interview here on one occasion couldn't answer and came back two months later and told the same story. So they really have no imagination. He said that Kalashnikovs were pointed to his chest but you couldn't see them because they were behind the cameras. And then I asked him why he hadn't said that before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I want to say something to Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, this question of CNN and the BBC stage managing these events is a serious allegation. Mr. Milosevic has explained how he sees the evidence as being relevant to the indictment. Regardless of whether you accept that or not, I think it is a matter that should be taken up in rebuttal so that these agencies have an opportunity to respond to these grave allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's the Court's view, then of course I'll reflect it, but I'd make this observation at this stage: Sensationalising news is irrelevant so far as this indictment is concerned. I have no cause, joint or otherwise, with CNN and BBC, although as a matter of courtesy to them I will pass on the allegations that are made. It would be my primary submission, and it may be something the Chamber will want to reflect on, that what is relevant is not what was made out of any particular incident by the BBC or CNN but what were the true reasons given by the refugees who were spoken to and who came and gave evidence here for their leaving Kosovo, and that's the real issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a matter for you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if a news agency is encouraging a certain form of behaviour, then it goes to undermine the point that you're trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only if it can be shown, I suppose, they've undermined the witnesses themselves. But I don't think -- well, that's a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should certainly pass it on to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But the connection between sensationalising news, if that happened, and undermining the evidence of the witnesses who have been called here or who have been spoken to by other agencies is, in my submission, either non-existent or tenuous in the extreme. But I'll pass the thing on to the BBC and CNN, and I'll of course respond to any specific invitation by the Court, perhaps later, to call evidence to deal with the problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, re-examination, and please remember re-examination is to deal with matters that arise in cross-examination. It's not an examination-in-chief all over again. And no leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one question, but before asking it I want to say for the record that you personally, Mr. Robinson, you personally here established playing the tape back several times that Mr. Nice showed that the BBC falsified even what I said in the translation they provided. So those are the same motives that Mr. Nice cannot seem to uncover. If they go so far as being -- as taking it upon themselves to translate incorrectly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have dealt with the matter in the way that I think it should be dealt with. Proceed with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Babik, Mr. Nice read something out to you from a book. It doesn't matter what the title of the book is. I think it is "Under Orders," that was the title of the book, I believe. And said that the Macedonian government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "As Seen, As Told" was the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The passage I read out was indeed from "Under Orders."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whereby the Macedonian government, from time to time waged a policy of force towards the Albanian refugees. You as a citizen of Macedonia, as an inhabitant of Macedonia, and as an employee of the health service working in the border belt, did you have any awareness at all of the fact that your country was waging a policy of violence towards the Albanian refugees?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: That's not true at all. Neither the Macedonian police nor the people there, the humanitarian workers, the people in the Red Cross, all of us there, there was just no violence there. That's not true. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the portion that wasn't translated to you we heard that the reporter said that that night eight people had died in the camp. Could that have happened without your knowing about it, because you were there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO BABIK
utterances.text: That could not have happened. Only one patient, to my knowledge, died. And to be more exact, on the 25th of May, that is one day prior to leaving, he died. However, he was seriously ill anyway. So I only know about that one patient. The others couldn't have happened without us knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Babik, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your next witness, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is Dietmar Hartwig.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, and to make use of every available second of time, it's perhaps worth having in mind that the issues that the accused is raising through those witnesses - I don't make a complaint about this but I observe - weren't raised with Prosecution witnesses who passed through Macedonian camps, I don't believe. One source of material that I can turn to to try and amplify the position of what happened in those camps and what may have been said by people in those camps is those very witnesses, and it's possible that if I can find out information from them I'll serve it 92 bis or serve it in some format for your consideration. I will try to deal with it as quickly as I can but these things always take time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the witness, I should like to ask you to bear in mind the fact that this is already the second German witness who, through force of circumstance, has been forced to testify in English, although the witness has asked for a German interpreter. That was the case with one of the previous witnesses too. The explanation was that there was no booth for German interpretation, and this witness speaks English but you should bear in mind that it would be easier for him to testify in German. This will not make this testimony not take place or happen slower, but I just would like to draw your attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpretation will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Interpretation is here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I've just been told that they will have German interpreters, because yesterday the situation and the explanation given to me was that they couldn't ensure a German interpreter to be present, but today I hear that they have been able to get one. Otherwise, I wouldn't have raised the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hartwig. Could you please tell me when and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: [In English] I was born 28 March 1939 in a town which is Poland today. On 7th May, 1947, we were expelled and we had to move to different places in -- I finished my school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you may give your testimony in German, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept in German. [Interpretation] I was born on the 28th of March, 1939, in a town that is now part of Poland. At the beginning of 1947, we were expelled from our homeland --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we are interested in that. Just bring him to the areas of his CV that would be relevant, Mr. Milosevic, so that we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Hartwig. You are a national of which country now?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I am a German national.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is, you were born in Germany and you are a German national.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I served 33 years in the German army. I was an upper lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from having spent 33 years in the German army, in the rank you mentioned, what positions -- in what positions did you serve?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: There were national uses in the integrated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand this answer.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: In national uses, I had officer staff functions and also command functions in which I worked, among other things. Also for nearly 10 years in different integrated positions in NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. It wasn't interpreted in full. Only a portion of your sentence had been interpreted earlier, so I couldn't really understand. Could you please tell me, in which period did you visit the former Yugoslavia? Which period or periods?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: My first stay in former Yugoslavia was from about October 1995 through to March 1996. Within the framework of the international conference of former Yugoslavia I had an observer mission. My second task was as part of the United Nations, as part of the return of east Slovenia to Croatia from May 1996 through to January 1998. And from July 1998 through to the end of October, beginning of November, I was as part of a European Observer Mission in Bosnia; and from there I went to the Kosovo where I was until the 19th of March, 1999, when we were evacuated to Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, if I understood you correctly, from November 1998 until the day of evacuation into Skopje on the 19th of March, you were in Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, according to this information, you headed the regional office of the monitoring mission of the European Union for Kosovo and Metohija. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: That is correct. I was manager of the regional office of the observer mission of the European Community in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This regional office that you had, the regional office of the monitoring mission, had in its purview the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: That is correct. And also I had teams in Mitrovica, Kosovska Mitrovica, in Prizren, in Orahovac, and in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional explanation, Mr. Hartwig, but I wanted first of all to establish one thing: You were head of the monitors of the European Union for Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Within the scope of this mission, I was certainly its manager of the office, the person responsible for the Kosovo region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. In which period exactly did you head the mission, the monitoring mission of the European Union for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I was head of this office officially from the 1st of January, 1999, through to the day of evacuation. Before that I -- for initial training, I spent about five weeks in Pristina beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, to make it quite clear to everyone, you in fact became head of the monitors on the 1st of January, that is the day when your country, Germany, took up the Presidency of the European Union. So your country became president of the European Union on the 1st of January, 1999, and you become the president -- or, rather, the head of the monitors for the European Union.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned that several weeks earlier you had arrived in Kosovo and Metohija for preparation, in order to get ready before you took up the regional office. Tell me, how long did this preparatory period last, and what did the preparations involve?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: The pure preparatory period, as I said, was about five weeks, and mainly I was concerned with finding a link to the mission up to this point of time and to learn about developments and to get information in order to quite simply obtain the necessary background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what you have said, your headquarters were in Pristina, and you had several regional centres that reported to you. That is, to put it most simply, the organisation within which you worked.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: The teams were virtually the external offices or the external offices of the main office, and every team, if possible, had to submit a report daily to the regional office, and this report, the main information was extracted from this report and this contributed to the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, because you said "were to report." I think they had the obligation to report to you daily on their observations as monitors. Did they in fact do that? Did you receive reports from your regional teams on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I received reports regularly, but I neglected this if perhaps there was nothing to report on any particular day. But I did receive reports regularly, and if there was nothing to report, then I simply submitted "nothing to report" and that was also a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. Could you tell me, please, in addition to the daily reports you received from the monitoring teams on the ground, did you yourself travel occasionally across Kosovo and Metohija in order to gain a personal insight into the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, I was travelling nearly every day, and on both sides, on the Albanian side and on the Yugoslav-Serbian side, I met all the people who in one form or another were involved in forming political decisions and who could make decisions, and I tried to get a balanced point of view from all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also in the preparatory period, because you told me right now what you did as of the 1st of January, but did you in the preparatory period, starting with November, have insight into the daily and other reports received from the field and the work of the monitoring teams?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: In the period before taking over, I also had a look at reports and also I had discussions on visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you also toured the area?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I was travelling in the whole region. I spent more time outside of the office than -- I think I would say I spent more time outside of the office than in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us, please, what was the mandate of the monitors of the entire mission you headed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, the mission was to look at the political, the economic, and religious aspects in Kosovo and to follow all this and, where possible, to find out where the focus was and to report this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your mandate was known under the acronym EUMM, European Union Monitoring Mission. It was known under that acronym; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That mandate of unbiased monitors, did it imply contacts with all the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: As far as I can judge this, I did this with all the people, in particular with the main parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were the people you contacted on the main sides involved? When I say "you," I mean also your monitors.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I personally talked to the Albanian side, to -- to Rugova. I talked to the designated vice-president of an independent Kosovo. Unfortunately, I cannot remember his name. I also talked to the leader of the Albanian university, Professor Kelmendi. I also talked to Dr. Jakobi about the legal implications of independence. I also talked with the chief editor and publisher of Kosovo Sot [phoen]. I also talked to somebody from Koha Ditore. I also talked to commanders of the KLA whose names I cannot remember. They were commanders, for example, at brigade level. And on several occasions I tried to meet a commander called Drini. Also travelled on my own with my interpreter to -- outside, but there was never a meeting on the Serbian side. I had a contact who was the leader of the Kosovo Verification Mission, General Loncar. Then also the head of the Kosovo security forces, General Lovric [as interpreted]. I also talked to the head of the Tribunal in Pristina --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hartwig. I suppose you said not Lovric but Lukic.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes, General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, with that correction, we will take the adjournment for 20 minutes. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, we left off after you described who your contact persons were on all the sides. Do you have anything to add as to the people you contacted on various sides?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I think I've mentioned the Albanian side completely. On the Serbian side I talked with Bishop Atimir [phoen], with the president of the kidnapped Serbs, and then the head of the Tribunal in Pristina, and some other persons whose functions and names I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Tribunal in Pristina," do you mean the district court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I assume it must be the district court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Hartwig, was it the task of the monitoring teams on the ground to find out as much as they can and to reflect in their reports what they heard and saw in the field?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, how often did you in your regional office in Pristina make reports that you sent to the headquarters of the monitoring missions in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Every day the teams would forward a report, and the regional office also sent a daily report to Sarajevo, which was set up with the various team reports and also with my information and observation. In addition, a weekly report was also put to Sarajevo, and moreover, on particular occasions we could also file special reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear about the reports now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand what you said, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was saying I think you have laid a sufficient foundation. Let us now hear what was reported to him, why he has come here to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify a couple of other points. Did you yourself write any reports?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes. At any rate, I drew up the weekly reports myself. As far as the procedure is concerned, I wrote them normally on my private laptop, and then I sent a final version which I then wrote on the -- on the office computer, which was then sent to the -- to the main office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps keep any of those reports or draft reports that you drafted on your laptop?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I kept some of the drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you keep all of them or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I suppose I have kept most of the drafts, but due to time pressure, I put them directly onto the office computer, but the majority, I assume I kept them on my laptop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Hartwig, what was the general impression and the generally accepted picture of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: At some stage I noticed that there was a contradiction between the image portrayed and reality. I also got this impression confirmed in conversations and with my personal observations. In our reports and in my report, we concentrated on facts, information -- information and data that were received from teams and that I -- I've learnt myself to use all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say there was a difference between what you saw and the image that was being created. Could you tell us in more detail what the difference was.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So, for example, in telephone conversations and in personal letters, I was made aware of situations and thinking, You must live in a terrible world; the Serbs are killing everybody. And I could only say it didn't happen in the region where I was based. I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This actual state of affairs that your own teams reported and that you could see with your own eyes, did they coincide with the generally accepted picture in the West or was there a difference?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So for my part, the most striking difference was after the return, after the evacuation to Germany where in the media I read about a picture of Kosovo, and I didn't think it had anything to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the image you encountered in the media after returning to Germany and that you say had nothing to do with reality?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Mainly it was the -- about the issue that events were taken out from their original context and that reporting was always very one-sided. There was only one perpetrator and always one victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the victim and who was the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: As the victims were normally Albanians and the perpetrators were normally deemed to be Serbians, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reality that you saw in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I didn't see it like that, and it wasn't my experience either, and I didn't see it in reports either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have any explanation? How did this inaccurate picture come about? How was it created?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation for that. I could only speculate, and I do not want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did this manipulation take place only in the West or was it helped also by Albanian media that launched it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Leading, and the witness has already declined to answer the general topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You'll have to ask the question differently, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, do I understand you correctly that you are saying there was a manipulation of public opinion? Just a simple yes or no would suffice.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: There was a stark contrast between the picture and reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which daily in the Albanian language, because we already talked about the Western press, was used by your mission to collect information and to compare with what you could see for yourselves?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: There was Koha Ditore for one thing. For some time it was also the Albanian edition of a newspaper called Times. Furthermore, we also received every morning from the Serbian and Albanian side, via fax, pieces of information. I cannot remember which news agency it was, but on the Albanian side it was mainly Koha Ditore and Times and the fax information. Also from the Serb side we got information from the information office and also via fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was -- what kind of reporting did Koha Ditore provide?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Koha Ditore was certainly, as far as its reporting was concerned, was Albanian oriented, and it certainly cannot be assumed that it can be -- that it should be unbiased. It clearly was in favour of the Albanian side and against the Serbian administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to purchase the daily Koha Ditore on a regular basis while you were in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I took over from my predecessor. I think he asked our driver to buy the newspaper, who then brought it to the office every day. That's why we received it every day on the day that it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to buy all the newspapers without any hindrance on the newsstands of Kosovo, particularly Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I don't know whether all newspapers would have been available. If I wanted, let's say, Newsweek, then I asked somebody to buy it in -- to buy it in the town, and then I usually also received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, are you aware of the existence and activity of various NGOs or similar organisations that transmitted an unrealistic, inaccurate picture of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Leading or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't agree, because he has already given evidence that in his view the general picture given was inaccurate and unrealistic. Yes. Answer the question. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think everybody who is little bit familiar with non-governmental organisation knows that they are also playing a part of politics, and this is not a criticism at all because it's their existence. Otherwise, they can't do any job. I think most of them, they, in a very plain and fair way, they tried to help others. Of course, they tried to take advantage of the situation. And I remember one case which might not be typical, but it was 8th of March in this time frame when in the radio I heard that Serbs had attacked three villages close to the Macedonian border, and that 4.000 refugees were waiting in front of the border crossing point Djeneral Jankovic, and by chance one of my teams was in that area and I radio -- excuse me. I -- [Interpretation] And then I asked them to go there and then to check things. And then they told me up to 3 or 400 people were there, whereas the NGO was talking about 4.000. Maybe it was just a mistake, but again you can notice that numbers are increased in order to achieve more flexibility in people's reactions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you also mentioned that allegedly three villages had been attacked and, if I understood well, they were destroyed and burnt down. Did your monitor check that as well?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the village Ivajakajlo [phoen] and Kotlina. And I heard it on the radio, and then went straight away to my car and drove there. I was also in one place called Ivaja. On the radio they said the villages are burning. And only about two hours later I was in Ivaja, and I saw a small fire there. Apart from that, the village was deserted, no people there. But it didn't look as if it had been destroyed. It was during the lunch break. Then I asked the team and tasked them to go back to the place a few days later, and I remember in the few days -- the few days later the report said roughly the villages have not been destroyed, but houses had been broken into, plundered partially, and there could be some fire -- some fire was detected in Ivaja. Ivaja was really the only village that was really destroyed. The other two villages had not been destroyed up until that point but only the houses had been plundered. And let's say fences, et cetera, were destroyed and parts of furniture, but that's what the report said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember a situation which confirmed your doubts or led you to doubt the truthfulness of what was happening and what was being said about the events in Kosovo and Metohija with respect to the generally accepted picture that was being painted, such as the -- and I mean the event, for example, that took place in Rogovo, the Rogovo case. Do you remember that? I'm asking you, Mr. Hartwig, just to make it quite clear, I'm asking you this because in certain documents I saw that the European monitors were there on the spot. Just if you remember. If you don't remember, you can say, "I don't remember," and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, I know about the Rogovo only a few details, and I'm not sure if my team was the first to be there. I only know that I received a report that 25 dead had been found and that some of them -- that some of them had the camouflage uniforms from the UCK, or the KLA. I know that afterwards I think there was an investigation, but as far as I know, nothing particular emerged from this, so I don't know what the outcome of this was, what the results were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, then, did you personally have a chance to attend the media sessions that were being made about the establishment of some kind of concentration camp for Albanians at the stadium in Pristina, for example?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I did not really get much note of the general reaction from the media, but at the beginning of March certainly I spent about a week -- an evening every week in this region, and our office was broken into this period, and among other things my camera and my films were stolen. But from a journalist I heard that such stolen goods occasionally were sold in the small shops near the stadium. And every evening I spend about half an hour or a quarter there and I took a look at this, and I also wanted to see if I could find my camera, but I didn't find anything. On the inside part of the stadium, I didn't see that anything unusual or illegal had in fact taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the news that was being put out that there was some kind of concentration camp over there for Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I certainly heard this, and I was very concerned about it. I'm not sure if I saw it on television or whether I heard it on radio or whether I had read about it, but I know that, yes, that there was mention of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
