utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milosevic. If I can go back to Rogovo incident. Mr. Hartwig, you mentioned that the 25 dead men, some of them had the camouflage uniforms from the UCK. I'm interested in the camouflage uniforms of KLA. How did they look like, and how do you know that they were camouflage uniforms of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my journeys through Kosovo repeatedly I was stopped at KLA posts, and I spoke to commanders of the UCK, or KLA. Where I was there were two different type of uniform. First of all, there was a camouflage uniform in -- well, at the moment I couldn't describe precisely what this looked like because the uniforms -- such uniforms look very similar throughout the world. And other -- another part of UCK had a black uniform without any particular pattern or without any particular pattern to it. So I know that there are camouflage uniforms all over the world, that these were not necessarily UCK people but certainly they were camouflage uniforms which were similar to those that were worn by the UCK, or KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But they were certainly uniforms, at any rate, not common clothing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, did you contact anyone, and if so whom, to ask for an explanation as to the major differences that occurred between what you could see on the ground in the field and what was being written by the media and the official versions that appeared in the West?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I think this question was put and not just once, but I never got an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you -- I do apologise. I'm not quite clear on the interpretation I was given. Did you raise the question? Because the question was raised neutrally, as -- it said, "I think this question was put." So that's neutral. Did you ask?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes. Also I asked my superior in Sarajevo where this came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your superior was the main -- the headquarters in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your question to the headquarters? What question did you ask them, did you ask the headquarters in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the exact wording of the question, but I certainly asked or I requested for an explanation whereupon we had this contradiction between reality and the way things were described. I asked for an explanation as to the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't receive an answer, as far as I was able to gather from what you just said.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: That is correct. I received no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, in the exhibits here, we have several texts which I'd like you to identify first, and then we can go on to deal with their contents. Would you take a look at tab 1 first, please. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it your text?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: It is my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us, please, when you wrote this text.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I probably wrote this immediately after my return from Germany. The essence of this was that the developments in Kosovo and the war that ensued, that I had been working on this within my mind, and it was necessary for me to put things down on paper, to also give my immediate assessment, my impressions and information. In other words, it was a type of -- for me, it was a paper in which I wrote down things to remind me about things that I had seen at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And so this aide-memoire, if I understand it, you wrote before the end of June 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that date at the latest. Is that right, Mr. Hartwig?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Before which day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the end of June 1999.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: In this period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to look at the document. And they are your personal observations set down in writing. And look at point 1. In point 1, you talk about the following: "What happened between the beginning of January and the 19th of March, 1999?" Or, rather, as far as I can see from this, you talk about what happened throughout the period of time that you headed the observer mission of the European Union in Kosovo and Metohija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now it says: "From the beginning of the year, an increasing number of attacks [In English] out of ambushes against Yugoslav security forces, rifle/grenade launcher and mortar fire against police stations and police officers, and later also against VJ could be recognised; in many cases Yugoslav police officers were killed, more frequently heavily wounded or sometimes kidnapped." [Interpretation] Did that come from the reports you received and from what you yourself saw when you were on the spot, in the field, that you were able to write your observations based on that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: My entire statements were not based on assumptions or things whispered to me but essentially I relied on information from the teams, and certainly in discussions I obtained background information, but what in total is described in the foreground, this was derived from official documentation, or semi-official documentation, and this can also be verified. There is evidence of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, I'm not clear as to exactly when you wrote this report. In response to Mr. Milosevic, you said sometime before June 1999. Are you able to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I cannot state the date with greater accuracy. It must be around the period immediately after the time when I started with this report. And I'm very sorry that I cannot give a definite statement on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would have been based on information that you received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And when would you have received that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information, for example, on attacks on police stations or also attacks on individual persons, this information I had within 24 hours on my desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So when you wrote the report, you consulted that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, because this was fresh in my mind, and I used this for my weekly reports. And with a great deal of luck, I was able to keep my diaries at the time in which I had noted daily events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you wrote this article with your computer, using word processor, and you kept the file in your laptop? Can you tell us when this document specific -- this one specifically was printed out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say. It may be that it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. printed out at a much later time. It is possible that I printed it out at a time later than the time when I was asked to come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move on, I observe that the witness said that the -- that this report's derived from official documentation or semi-official documentation. This can also be verified. Now, the documentation of his mission is material that I would have expected him to have brought with him. If he has and if I have a chance to look at it, I will be able to deal with it more fully and more satisfactorily in cross-examination. If he hasn't brought it with him, I have to tell the Court that the material is not available to be me in a form that I can use. We have some material from his mission and, subject to restriction, we have brought them but only for the purposes of ensuring that the accused has the material to which he is entitled under Rule 68. So if the witness who says he was the senior official in this mission hasn't brought the supporting material, I'm going to be in that difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. We hear the submissions. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just something with respect to that, another explanation, Mr. Hartwig, please. How did it come about that part of your documents were destroyed in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I had a small collection of personal notes that I had made, and in mid-March I was away for some time, and in this period some of my teams from the team locations were evacuated to Skopje and also part of my office, and in this context, some of my personal notes were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. Now, let's go back for a moment to tab 1. You go on to say the following: "Additionally, there was an increasing number of actions [In English] against installations in cities known as social meeting points of Serbs (hand grenades in cafes or bars, rifle fire at guests - e.g. Pristina, Pec, Djakovica, et cetera); so far, similar actions only happened outside villages and towns." [Interpretation] You go on to say, "The 'normal' -" the normal is under inverted commas - "The 'normal' killing of Serb civilians [In English] or of Albanians suspected to cooperate with Serbs or to work for Serbs or Serbian companies, Yugoslav administration continued..." [Interpretation] And then you say, the "(11 February the OSCE reported that 10 Albanians were kidnapped by UCK due to suspected relations with Serbs) [In English] or even increased." [Interpretation] Were all these events which you were able to follow on a daily basis in your capacity as head of the European monitors in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: As I've already said, I always heard about these incidents at the latest 24 hours after the event, and hence I was always updated. Then you talked about the -- what was said in inverted commas, the "normal" killing, that reflects my personal impression, because the whole atmosphere was so tense that the death of a person as such was considered to be something normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You then go on to speak in this text of yours about the following: "[In English] On 24th of January, UCK tried to create pressure on the international community --" [Interpretation] and then in brackets "IC" -- "UCK is ready to resort to a more active campaign should IC not respond to Racak into tangible and early benefits of the Albanian case."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On January 24th, the sentence begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain that to us more closely, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I know that in a statement, I think I read it, that the KLA announced that they would be harsher if the international community would draw clearer consequences from what happened in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, since we haven't got time to go through the entire text, I should just like to draw your attention to a couple of other things. At the bottom of page 1 you say the following: "[In English] I would like to stress the point that - always only until 19 March 1999 - Yugoslav security forces and VJ reacted very disciplined and controlled on attacks and provocations by UCK. On the other hand, as soon as Yugoslav Security Forces or VJ reacted on UCK attacks or provocations, UCK loudly and skilfully blamed the Serbs/Yugoslav publicly for arbitrary actions. "Tactics and operations in a conflict against an underground army unfortunately do not allow for a lot of consideration of human lifes or the opinion of nations not directly concerned." [Interpretation] Therefore, you were talking about, and I'd like to extract that point, about the fact that the Yugoslav forces, that is to say the security forces and the army, you say, reacted very disciplined and controlled on attacks and provocations by the UCK. Could you explain that to us more fully, please. What do you mean by it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm still not clear about what is called here a report, tab 1. Was this a report, Mr. Hartwig, that you prepared for onward transmission to a body or was it for your own personal purposes, private purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was basically for my own personal purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. And what we have here is a translation, then. It would have been in German. In English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly must have written it in English. Just to explain, I did write in English straight away in order to practice my English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you've done quite well. Continue, Mr. Milosevic. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have in mind the fact that Mr. Hartwig was the head of the monitoring mission of the European Union and that he is talking about what he saw personally and also what he learnt on the basis of the reports from his team, and it is he himself who is testifying, and we have established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My question was prompted by the description of tab 1 as a draft report, which suggests that it was prepared for transmission to some authority. In fact, it was -- as it has turned out, it is Mr. Hartwig's own assessment of the situation in Kosovo for his own private purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I -- that doesn't diminish the importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't said that at all. I just need to be clear as to what it is that we're looking at. Mr. Hartwig, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Originally I considered it to be my personal document. After the war, I also asked for a talk back home in order to give the background of my report, and if I had had -- took such a meeting with somebody, I certainly would have used this report, but it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we were saying, Mr. Hartwig, from what you observed here, it would emerge that the army or, rather, the security forces, always responded to provocations, and you say provocations by UCK. Then whenever there was a response to the provocations, the army and the police were accused of arbitrary violence. Would that be an accurate description of what you were able to see on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Basically it's precisely the kind of guerrilla tactics that were used, that from an ambush fighting started, and then the fighters would withdraw as quickly as possible and then watch or behave normally, so that if further investigations were carried out, no links could be established. Apart from that, it was my clear -- it was my clear -- I had a clear impression that a provocation had taken place, and if the security forces reacted to such provocations, they were accused of acting arbitrarily. If I can just give you a little personal history. Sometimes my little sister annoyed me very much. And when I wanted to react to it, she immediately started crying, and I was the bad one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, I'll try to move on as fast as I can but not at the cost of skipping over important facts. Look at page 2. You say that after you arrived in Pristina, in relation to this paragraph A(1), you say after your arrival in Pristina, you talked one after another to all the members of the Western mission, and you say: "[In English] I was told by all of them, I was told by all of them that there was a clear contradiction between their reports into their capitals (governments) and the Kosovo situation published by their governments." [Interpretation] Was that the rule, the phenomenon you could observe throughout your stay in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: That is first experienced from meetings I had with the members of the various nations that certainly has made me very sensitive and alerted me to something that -- something that you had to be aware of that. It wasn't on a daily basis, but whenever I had the opportunity, I could note that they -- these differences that we talked about at the beginning, that is the contrast between what really happened and how it was then reported, that this -- there was this difference. This contrast did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the next sentence reads: "So far, I fully agree to your link between the late NATO engagement in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the early/unjustified NATO commitment in Kosovo." Mr. Hartwig, "your link" suggests that you were referring to a link made by somebody else. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no -- no clear particular person whatsoever. I just tried to develop, to describe my feelings, my considerations, somehow my -- my idea, and it was something I just used. Somebody would -- does not physically exist. It was like a dispute with a shadow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You could have said easily "to a link."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I had known that it will be the subject of a case in front of a court, I would have probably used very careful words. It was at this time something that I never thought would be used. No, it was really nothing which was assigned to be sent to somebody. It was a collection of thoughts to describe my feelings, my concerns as well of the situation. And as mentioned, it was never originally -- it was not signed to be published or something like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, that is the second numbered paragraph in a section which starts or is headed "To a." and then over the page we have "To b." Were these questions which were posed that you were answering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I had something, a scheme on a draft paper that I used, manually written, a type of guideline, what would you like to think about, the sequence of paragraphs that I referred to that manual draft paper. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And just beneath 2 perhaps is the explanation. It says: "Before this main point, more easier questions need to be answered: A. What did really happen? B. What was reported by the media..." I suggest that those are questions he had set himself. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I had initially skipped over this point "2. 'Cui bono' the old Romans asked..." What did really happen and what was reported by the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, under A, you say, "As indicated earlier already, [In English] until 19 March 1999 there were no reasons at all to anybody to interfere with the Yugoslav Administration in the Kosovo. "All leading politicians and on request of OSCE the Head of the Yugoslav Kosovo Verification Mission successfully tried to retain control of the security forces and the VJ which were very much upset and excited of the permanent attacks, provocations, pin-pricks by UCK and numerous killings of colleagues without any opportunity of a legal retaliation." [Interpretation] And then in brackets we read "underground army." And then in point 3 you say: "Within the Yugoslav security forces, there were not only Serbs, but also Albanians who were specifically targets of UCK due to their clear cooperation with the Serbs." Mr. Hartwig, could you give us a comment on this? Establish a link with what you personally found to be the case as head of the monitoring mission in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just quoted point 2, where you said, "As indicated earlier already, until 19 March 1999 --" that is practically until the end of your mission, until your withdrawal -- "there was no reason at all for anybody to interfere with the Yugoslav administration in Kosovo." So your entire experience as head of European monitors indicates that there was no reason for such interference. Is that your basic conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So on the basis on that what I've seen, what I've experienced, what I got in terms of information, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us cover very briefly. At the end of this point A, you say: "One aspect hasn't been mentioned at all so far: [In English] The rivalry between the old and traditional Albanian clans living in Kosovo. They did not cooperate, there was no 'time out' for their traditional revenge ... and they most probably used the critical situation to strengthen their positions. There was a saying that one mass grave in the vicinity of Srbica (approximately 40 dead bodies) was the result of clan 'competition' - albeit the Serbs were blamed for." [Interpretation] How did you manage to establish this and how did you arrive at these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I think we're talking about the mass grave. I went there, and I heard that this mass grave was filled with people killed by the Serbs, and I'm not sure who actually killed them, but I spoke to people not specifically with respect to Donje Crnje [phoen] but in discussions I'm not quite sure with whom, suddenly someone told me that the dead people of Donje Brnje [phoen] were not victims of a Serbian attack but that this was an armed dispute between two clans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is there an allegation in the indictment about Srbica, the mass grave there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll check it. I'll check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm asking, I'm trying to find out whether there's an allegation, because you must bear in mind, Mr. Milosevic, you will strengthen your case if this witness, who was with the ECMM, can give specific information on the basis of reports made to him such as this, which would contradict anything in the indictment. That would be much more helpful than merely getting his general observations about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 66(G) Srbica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is not only about Srbica. The point here that everything that happened was ascribed to the Serbian side, all the killings, although there were many conflicts, and here the witness, I'm quoting paragraph 3. According to the data we had, Albanian terrorists killed more Albanians than Serbs did. The paragraph 3 was in item A, "Within the Yugoslav security forces, there were not only Serbs, but also Albanians - which were specifically targets of KLA due to their clear cooperation with the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is an allegation in 66(G) that relates to Srbica. Or is it Ivica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the municipality of Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is in 63(C) a reference to Srbica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look now at what you wrote until -- under subitem B. You explain: "For quite some time nobody paid any attention as to what was going on in Kosovo. Perhaps it was the tiredness of the Europeans after their energy consuming decision to task NATO to intervene in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But suddenly Kosovo became a subject; reports were increasingly published talking of the suppression of Albanians by the Yugoslav/Serb administration, attacks against Albanians, arsons against Albanian houses, discrimination against Albanians in companies, schools, et cetera. "After the experience with 'the Serbs' in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were no doubts at all that those reports were true. But there was no European reaction - until the media brought the story of ethnical cleansing and atrocities against Albanians." Thus, Mr. Hartwig, what we have here is an easily marketable story that Serbs were committing crimes, and the story was launched without any real grounds. Was that what you were able to establish and testify to?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, I repeat that on the basis of my observations, the statement is correct that many crimes or that a lot was ascribed to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was easy to believe for everyone thanks, among other things, to the propaganda.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, I agree that the fact of presenting someone immediately and on the spot, of finding a culprit immediately, this makes life easier for many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look further below. "[In english] It is to be assumed that at this time already a political plan existed to look for an opportunity to attack Kosovo; since no political goal for a commitment of military power could be offered to the public, big-scale atrocities were required. "Everything reported by Albanians was gratefully accepted." Gratefully. "Balanced reporting became a foreign word. I do not want to be misunderstood: I am very much in favour of clear reporting in the case of crimes or atrocities - if they are reality; I am strongly against any manipulation of situations, statements or reports." [Interpretation] Then you say: "When I did my courtesy calls to Serbian political and clerical leaders (I did the very same to the Albanians, too), I was always 'the first European.' [In English] It is, therefore, no miracle that the interviews and reports were rather one-sided and by no means impartial - but, obviously, they were not intended to be objective." [Interpretation] Then you say: "The main point in most of the interviews prior to the NATO air attacks seemed to obtain a picture as bad as possible [In English] and to show YU as ugly as feasible. The media reported everything and to the very last detail - the worse, the better. "Ordinary people couldn't differ between propaganda and reality - though politicians declared stories honest and true. "It was imperative to report of or to show atrocities - the worse the easier it was to the media to justify any own/NATO military commitment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have taken up almost a whole page of the transcript just reading. It's time for a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish with this sentence: "The prescription worked - and today it is believed that it was the media that failed. They were not a control element of politics but compliant servants."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hartwig, according to what you were able to see, was there a parallel media war that was leading to and enabling a real military intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I wonder really whether that sort of question is the right side of the line. I've noticed a number of leading questions which I haven't objected to, and the witness is quite cautious about the way he answers, but I wonder if characterising his state of mind in that way is really helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, at the time -- at the time when you were formulating these observations of yours, how were you able to assess the relationship between the media campaign and the military campaign?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I think quite simply, because today it is not easily possible to start a war. Today wars must be prepared on the basis of previous experience in some way, and to prepare a war, in my opinion, it is necessary to find some facts that support this, and therefore I believe that it is a possibility and certainly it is a historically proven or tried possibility if the things really have occurred or if they are developed to a fantasy, if these things are presented in such a clear or overclear way that a simple man on the street can see a reason for taking military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say at the end of this paragraph 1: "Until the commencement of NATO air attacks on Kosovo, the Serbs did not expel people out of Kosovo." Since you've just commented upon the portion quoted previously, the prescription worked and it is considered today that the media failed. And on the next page you say: "The campaign only makes sense if the above question can be answered. Is it really realistic to assume that human rights were defended or restored? Were there clear facts to prove that the Serbs (basically the Yugoslav army - VJ - and MUP units) really committed crimes against other ethnical groups prior to the commencement of NATO air attacks? Or were the media only compliant servants of politics and reported what the politicians wanted them to report? [In English] If this should be the case, it would be of interest to know who there was interested in providing a manipulated or even wrong picture of the situation on the Kosovo to the public." [Interpretation] Does this need additional comment, Mr. Hartwig, or is it a clear attitude, clear belief of yours that you recorded in this text?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, it was or it is a very clear, or even to the limit of the permissible description of what I have seen and experienced. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you conclude by saying, "This indicates [In English] that the contention to 'defend human rights' et cetera and to avoid a human catastrophe in front of the European Community are neither true nor honest." [Interpretation] Let us note once again, Mr. Hartwig, you wrote this in 1999, at the time when you headed the European Monitoring Mission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I don't think in the -- I don't think I wrote this at the time, the active time when I was head of the mission, but later. I produced this collection at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1999.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You told us earlier this was prior to June 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A major part for sure. I -- as mentioned, it was not -- [No interpretation] [Interpretation] ... a draft paper and Serbs would put them down on paper and followed them. And I do not -- cannot exclude then on occasions I changed the wording of some sentences, but the paper as such was worded at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you do with the paper? Did you make any use of it after you wrote this? It's obviously strongly held views.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't use that document, but on occasions in discussions, in personal discussions but not in public but in personal conversations that I had I did explain the experience that I've had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't think I'll be returning to tab 1. I'd like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, we're going to go on to tab 2 now, please. I hope we'll be able to get through that quicker. Would you have a look at that exhibit now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the court deputy give the number for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The whole binder will be D283.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you have tab 2 in front of you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, is this your presentation, the one you gave, the one you delivered to the European Union?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: This is the text of a presentation that I held at a conference in Sarajevo in front of staff of the mission headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us about this conference. Who organised it, under whose auspices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of the year 1999, the Federal Republic of Germany had the Presidency of the European Union. At that moment in time, a German head of mission was also set in -- set up. And at the time, within these six months, he set up this conference where particular matters were debated. And as I came from Kosovo, I was tasked to portray the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the general purpose of the conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an exchange of information, update -- general update to inform people about the state of affairs which emphasis was supposed to be put over the next six months. It was for people who had been dealing with the history of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just explain the first page. It says German Presidency of the ECMM, 1st January 1999 to 30th June 1999. That is the period of time when Germany presided; is that right? It's just an indication of the period of time that the German Presidency was in force for.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "AOR" means "area of responsibility"; right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: [In English] Responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the internal memorandum, you submitted that on the 16th of March, 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I must have put it forward about a week in advance. The conference was on the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we've clarified all that now. The conference was held on the 16th of March, and this internal memorandum you sent in to them one week prior to that. Now, using this internal memorandum, did you present an oral presentation at the conference on the situation on Kosovo and Metohija. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes, I did that presentation. I made that presentation, based myself on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll just skim through it briefly, I hope. In the first sentence, this is what you say. The title is "Situation on the ground in Kosovo." "[In English] Generally, the situation is different to the picture provided by media - and in reality it also differs between ethnic and social groups. "The media demonstrate their philosophy to promote news according to their own political position - and do not always pay attention to a complete and true and honest picture." [Interpretation] So that position taken by you which we were able to see through the previous document we looked at, you are now presenting at a public conference; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: It wasn't a public conference, but it was a conference in front of the staff of the observers mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, I understand that correction. You mean that the journalists weren't present, but it was an official conference with the participation of all those involved in the observer missions, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Observers as well as administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the format of the presentation? Were questions asked after the presentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we heard. The "AOR" is abbreviation of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many participants were there at the conference?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: [In English] Between 40 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When I say that you publicly presented your views and positions, I mean publicly before those 40 or 60 people who attended; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's your own definition of public, Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let me say official, then, because it was a conference and the conference was officially held.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You state here the following: "Kosovo Albanians, to a big degree, are not politically interested [In English] or just political trimmers without an own political opinion - following every LDK or KLA statement promising a better life. "Only a small part of the Kosovo Albanians is - more or less - politically engaged, deals with political ideas which not yet have clearly been identified. Even worse, Kosovo Albanians could not agree upon one political representation or representative who was entitled to speak on behalf of most of the Albanians." [Interpretation] Then you go on to explain what the radical part does of the Kosovo Albanians, mainly represented by the KLA. And you go on to list the political objective, as you say, and the first point you set down is to get rid of the Serbian ruled administration. And then you go on to say, to get completely rid of all Serbs within Kosovo. And then you go on to explain who it is who expresses this, as indicated by: "[In English] To establish an Albanian Kosovo - with a hidden view on the Albanians in former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and Montenegro -" [Interpretation] that's the next objective - "[In English] and a unification with the these parts." [Interpretation] In your explanations, did you use the term or did you know of the term "Greater Albania"?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I have used the term "Greater Albania," as far as I recall, on one occasion, when I drew a comparison where on the one -- where I said on the one hand the idea of a Greater Serbia or -- is going -- is considered as a reality, and nobody says anything about what I've heard in conversations with Albanians, that is the restoration of an Albanian Empire within medieval restraints, frontiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is fully what you say -- not fully but partially when you say, "Establish an Albanian Kosovo - with a hidden view on the Albanians in [In English] the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and Montenegro - unification with these parts." [Interpretation] Is that a partial description of what you implied by the concept or notion of Greater Albania?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: When I talk about the Greater Albania and its historic concepts, that did include today's state of Albania. At the time in Kosovo when I had meetings with Albanians and talked to them, they referred to the Macedonian part of Albania and Montenegro. So I had the impression that the citizens of the state of Albania are considered to be the poor cousin of the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to speak of the following, the Serbs -- next title. And you go on to describe the situation with the Serbs, that the Serbs speak about political mistakes made in '89, "... the political mistake of 1989 when the autonomy was withdrawn from Kosovo by Milosevic; [In English] and almost all of the politicians in office met would be willing to participate in discussions with the moderate Albanians on the organisation of the future..." on the organisation of the future. [Interpretation] So that, then, was the general mood that prevailed and which you noted in your contacts with the Serb officials you met in Kosovo. Is that right, Mr. Hartwig?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So what I wrote with regard to the withdrawal of autonomy, that was my understanding on two or three occasions. But what I generally noted in my conversations was this very strong need in order to create a situation which for the Serbs and also for the other ethnic groups in Kosovo there would be a basis for co-existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was the position of the Serbs that you talked to, was it?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, you go on to say the following: "[In English] The increasing expansion of UCK and their 'terrorist attacks' in guerrilla tactics against police, civilians and VJ hardened the positions of even moderate Serbs and decreased the willingness to negotiate. Western media and politicians, in the view of Serbs - not only Kosovo Serbs - supported that development by an inappropriate public and political acknowledgement of and attention paid to KLA, their leaders, and permanently blaming only one side - the Serbs. It is not for our fun or voluntariness - we are obliged by law to protect people and to guarantee law and order; we do it in our way. What would happen in your country if police patrols were ambushed, policemen assassinated or bombs thrown into cafes or restaurants? Would your police just observe? - These were the questions of the head of the Kosovo police force to me." [Interpretation] Therefore, Mr. Hartwig, at the time, and this is happening on the 16th of March, you prepared this one week before that or somewhat more in advance because you sent it in a week before, but anyway, this is the situation in which we see confirmation -- or, rather, let me ask you: Is this an assertion which confirms that what we were dealing with was an escalation of terrorist attacks of the KLA against the objectives in Kosovo and Metohija, targets in Kosovo and Metohija; the police, the army, civilians and other targets; restaurants, cafes, and all the other things mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the Chamber happy with that sort of question? It would seem to me again it's pretty well giving the entire answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement, there's certainly the facts from reports and from other sources of information which were gained from an intensified number of attacks of the executive power and against the Serb authorities. It was quite interesting that when negotiations started, the number of incidents per day increased. And you can -- that was also -- and that was also reflected in my report even if it doesn't say so explicitly here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, could I ask you what you mean by the comment or the question, "What would happen in your country if police patrols were ambushed, policemen assassinated or bombs thrown into cafes or restaurants? What would your --" sorry -- "Would your police just observe?" What was the point of these comments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote that basically in order to portray the situation of the Serb executive. These questions come from a conversation with General Lukic, and he asked these questions. And he said, "How would people react in your country to a situation like this?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did that observation sound to you like an attempt at justification for retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have that impression at all. And during my time in Kosovo, I didn't have the impression that the police or the military -- I did have the impression that to stick to the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement. And I had another conversation with General Lukic, and on that occasion he said we could use -- we were under different circumstances. We could cope with the KLA, but we do not want to be a party -- a contractual party who could be deemed to be not reliable. So there was the aspiration by complying with the agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke to really comply with it as fully as possible in order not to create any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, Mr. Bonomy mentioned the word "retaliation" a moment ago. Did you anywhere during your stay in Kosovo have the impression that the police or the army entered into any type of retaliation, that it was -- that it engaged in an action that could be defined as retaliation? Did you gain that impression ever?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I didn't receive any single report in which there was even an indication of anything like this having been said. My own personal impression was -- was similar. I personally had -- I personally did not hear of revenge, and it was not said in many discussions with Albanians. Actually, there was never any indication that the police in general, or that certain policemen or military personnel had done anything that was illegal. But on questioning them, they spoke rather more generally. People were arrested by the Serbian police, and they were put into prison, and we do not know where they are. But there was no clear reference, nor was there any indication in the report that somewhere revenge had taken place. And I personally would like to add this does not exclude the possibility that in individual cases perhaps something did happen, as is always possible where so many people are involved. Perhaps a single incident did occur. But the way it is described there, that something had been commanded from a high level, that revenge actions had taken place, I know nothing about anything of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. You then go on to speak here -- or, rather, you inform about the KLA military: "[In English] The UCK attack against a police patrol in the village of Likosani on 28 February 1998 ..." [Interpretation] That was the beginning, when two policemen were killed, two wounded, and so on and so forth. And then you go on and say, "Since then, KLA guerrilla tactics have developed [In English] and operations improved - together with the material status of light infantry weapons. Military training - unitwise already, status of skills and force organisation improved and fighting and supporting personnel numbers increased." [Interpretation] Then you go on to say: "[In English] The rector of the Albanian university Pristina announced that he is happy of every student who joins or who will join the KLA." [Interpretation] How did you come to learn of that?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Because I had a talk with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. So that means from direct contact; right? Thank you. "[In English] Police/MUP stations and patrols remained main targets during the last year - while VJ remained untouched till the end of 1998; this changed in 1999 when repeatedly VJ convoys were attacked by KLA which more and more tries to dictate courses of actions." [Interpretation] How did you then deduce and draw the conclusions as to what the goal was of the KLA, and did you have any knowledge at all about any conflict that was initiated by the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: The second question first. I know of no conflict that was initiated, and I did not receive any reports, and I myself had seen nothing or heard anything. As regards the question of the goals of the KLA, my impression was that the UCK, the KLA, because of their action, to some extent deliberately accepted that damage or that harm would occur to their own people, the Kosovo conflict, and they tried to keep the conflict in Kosovo alive in the eyes of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You then go on to give two examples. One example, in the second paragraph, where you say the following: "[In English] One example is when a Serb investigation team from Pristina was shot at by KLA and five MUP were wounded --" MUP means policemen -- "were wounded while trying to gather evidence of a murder of one Serb and the wounding of another two Serbs on 22nd and 23rd of February respectively at Bukos; the media excessively reported of the MUP reaction of that incident." [Interpretation] Is that one example of this complete distortion in reporting?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I assumed that this was less due to the report although you could see it in that way, but I recorded it because of the expansion of the KLA and the -- and this also made clear the growth in their forces. Meanwhile, it had become clear that not just the state executive, whether one was satisfied with them or not, that the executive maintained the law, but that an illegal troop was responsible for upholding the law. And in March 1999, I had to make great efforts to get a police team to us in the office in Pristina because -- Pristina, because the police also did not feel very sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, what do you mean by "The media excessively reported the MUP reaction to that incident"? What was the reaction of the MUP that they were reporting excessively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason behind that statement -- [Interpretation] The background to this is the following: In the initial period, many journalists came -- that were visiting Kosovo, came to us in the office to get information on the situation, and during this time journalists in general came or went mainly to the Albanians and obtained information on the situation, and this necessarily meant that the one side where they got more information was reported on in more detail, and in talks with people on the Serbian side that were involved in public relations, I found that here hardly anyone was interested in the other side of a version or of an event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to give a fairly extensive explanation about the functioning or, rather, the evolvement of the operations themselves in the last paragraph on the page I'm quoting from. So in your report you say the following: "[In English] Village by village is infiltrated, villagers are voluntarily or forcibly convinced to join - or to at support at least." [Interpretation] And you're referring to the KLA. "[In English] As soon as the advance of KLA is known to the police, the village becomes a potential target. Should there be any incidents in the close proximity to that village, police will automatically assume the perpetrators are from there - and take action. Actions against guerrilla fighters are the most difficult military operations and, therefore, something like an area covering action seems to be the only means. There is a method behind: The international community, of course, sympathises with Albanians and KLA when TV pictures can be presented showing civilians killed or villages destroyed - regardless of whether it was an action or reaction conducted by security forces. "Finally, the liberation of KLA and the potential search or retaliation by Serb security forces turn out to become a vicious circle to the villagers; their alternative might be to either be killed by KLA - or by Serb security forces." [Interpretation] Faced with a situation like that, did you happen to note a phenomenon by which when the KLA comes into a village and occupies it, takes control of it and starts launching its provocations and ambushes of the police and others, that the civilians leave that village? They tend to take refuge, leave the village and take refuge somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the reference to "starts launching its provocations and ambushes of the police," the question is leading and you will have to reformulate it. It is my view that you do not exercise sufficient discipline in your examination-in-chief, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say, and I'm going to read another passage -- not to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ask leading questions, I'm going to quote your own text: "[In English] Should there be any incidents in close proximity to that village --" [Interpretation] When you say incidents in the close proximity to a village, do you mean an incident which is caused by the police or do you have in mind incidents caused by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Well, certainly there were no incidents that had been provoked by the police. These were incidents where -- which resulted in the police reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, where are you reading from? What page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I re-read something that I've read before. It's in the middle of the page I earlier read from, and then I came back to it. "Should there be incidents in the close proximity of that village." It's in the middle of the last paragraph on that page, paragraph starting with "KLA ..." and I asked Mr. Hartwig whether it would be an incident caused by the KLA or by the police, and Mr. Hartwig answered that it was an incident caused by the KLA. And now I hope I can ask a question which is not provocative or, rather, isn't leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whenever an incident would occur, such as an ambush, killing of a policeman or a serviceman, followed by a clash, did you notice perhaps whether the civilians from the villages, tend to take cover, to leave the village or the area in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to ask him what did the civilians from the villages do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson. Let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the civilians do?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: As a rule, in accordance with our observation, it was not such that a policeman was shot, and that will certainly -- if a shooting had taken place, that of course people shot back, but this inclusion of the villages resulted frequently much later when -- if the police tried to get hold of the culprit. Then the situation was that the villagers, the inhabitants of the village then found themselves in the crossfire because those that attacked the police and then they were caught in the reaction, shooting from the security forces, and frequently this was the reason why, if there was any indication of something like this, that the civilian people left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. That is the only thing I wanted to hear from you. In your contacts with the police administration in Kosovo, did you have opportunity to hear anything about the concern and efforts and orders issued by the police to -- aimed at avoiding civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Now, I did not experience any such commands being issued, but at least in discussions I obtained the clear impression that one really did try to ensure that every kind of attention, or one wanted to avoid attention in the world which would lead to further worsening of the Serbian reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hartwig. You speak here specifically about the police. "MUP, the federal police under command of the Ministry of the Interior, supports normal Traffic Police. Independently, there are stationary MUP-controlled points along predetermined roads. [In English] Apart of general observation and traffic control activities, MUP is the means to conduct semi-military operations within and around villages; the training status is high, discipline is told to be high, and equipment consists of armoured vehicle, automatic guns and light infantry weapons." [Interpretation] Then you go on to say: "... MUP sub-units or units are committed against KLA elements to prevent or to follow actions and in patrolling throughout dangerous areas." So reference is made here to the KLA and the problems experienced by the police with the KLA as well as the origin of incidents. Do you know of any incident from your personal experience or from reports wherein the police attacked civilians?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: I've already said so. I didn't -- I don't know any -- I don't know anything of such incidents. If I interpret that the police would carry out an attack against the civilian population without a specific reason, then I do not know of any such incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you explain here further below, speaking of the humanitarian situation, after the sub-heading "Humanitarian situation," in the second paragraph: "Refugee numbers vary extremely; in the first week of March, UNHCR reported some 3.000 refugees and more in the area of Djeneral Jankovic border crossing along the road Pristina-Skopje. [In English] We had a team there twice - and the members never counted more than 300 to 400 people. After MUP actions, UNHCR publishes refugee numbers which exceeded the number of inhabitants of the village sometimes by two or three times. This is partially caused by the sheltering of refugees by local inhabitants." [Interpretation] Could you please tell us, on the basis of your knowledge, why would the UNHCR increase the number of refugees almost tenfold? For instance, we have reference to 3.000 as reported by UNHCR as opposed to 300 or 400 that you actually found on the ground.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: As I've already said, I do not know the real reason, but I've only got one or two possible explanations for that. For one thing, it could be that UNHCR relied on statements made by people who were on site. It might be villagers who might have said so. On the other hand, as far as humanitarian aid is concerned, there's always the question of numbers, as far as aid is concerned. So there are only two explanations to this, in my opinion: Either in the heat of the moment somebody just gave a figure, but you cannot exclude the intention then, when giving a larger number, you might get a -- more room for manoeuvre. But this is only speculation, and I would like to take it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I will not press you on this. Tell me, Mr. Hartwig, was there any relationship or cooperation between your monitoring mission and the Verification Mission of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Let me say it differently. Our mission already existed in Kosovo when the OSCE was set up. So our mission already existed before the OSCE was set up in Kosovo. In the preliminary phase, we helped with setting it up and also sent along reports. So our working level cooperation was the usual in international posts. Sometimes there were particular problems relating to the profession. Each military commander has got its area of responsibility, and whoever comes in from the outside is a subordinate. And we were in Kosovo in the OSCE area, and we were not subordinates, which meant that General Dizat [phoen], he would have liked us to be under his command but that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your mission was independent of the OSCE Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: Yes. We were completely independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to move on to another subject. If you could tell us very briefly about what you know from your experience and your contacts with the representatives of the administration, the Serb administration in Kosovo and in Serbia, and the representatives of Kosovo Albanians. What were the authorities of Serbia seeking to achieve, and what were the goals of the Kosovo Albanian leadership as you heard from KLA leadership that you met? You were in contact with both sides.

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So the authorities within Kosovo were already -- already existed. I talked to ministers, to other representatives. And as I've already stated, there was a clear aspiration that was noticeable in order to find a peaceful and a solution which would be acceptable to all sides. That was different on the Albanian side, because there, right from the beginning, the independence of Kosovo existed as the objective, and I -- I didn't get a description of this kind of independence of Kosovo in conjunction of Serb presence. It was mainly pointed out by the designated vice-president of independent Kosovo, not with the Serbs and not under the Serbs, because the Serbs would not give any rights to minorities; hence, the objective stated was independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this very clear answer. Just one more thing. Was the purpose of eliminating Serbs - and you used the expression "getting rid of the Serbs" - only to become an independent part, independent of Serbia and Yugoslavia, or was it also desirable to eliminate Serbs from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So after the conversations I had, the objective was clearly to have a Kosovo with exclusive -- with an exclusive Albanian administration. There was no deviation or there were no differences in ideas. Kosovo without Yugoslavia independent. I talked to Dr. Jakobi and asked him what independence should mean in that context because in such a small country as Kosovo with 11.000 square kilometres, economic independence would be difficult to imagine, and I occasionally had the impression that this term "independence" can be interpreted quite differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what way differently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how much longer do you plan to be? You had estimated, I see here, two hours. At the rate at which we are going, you will probably need two or three times that. Progress has been very slow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope I can finish within another hour, at least the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have another ten minutes, so use it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got a few matters that I'd like to raise, probably about five minutes in all, two of them concerning this witness, two not. No more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another five minutes, because we have to stop at 1.45 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A very straightforward question: Did this interpretation of the independent Kosovo imply, on the basis of the conversations you had and the knowledge you had, did it imply elimination of Serbs from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So the statement made by the vice-president not with -- not under the Serbs -- not with the Serbs implies to me quite clearly that no peaceful co-existence was envisaged with the Serbs. "Not with the Serbs" meant out of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you spent almost six months in Pristina. Let me not engage in guesswork. You were there from November until the 15th of March without interruption. What was the situation in town during the time you were in Pristina, including the preparatory period and during your term of office as leader of European monitors? What was the situation in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: So regardless of the fact that I couldn't cope with the language, I moved around Pristina as I would move around other towns as well. I didn't feel threatened, nor did I feel in -- under any risk. You could also go out and have a meal somewhere in the evenings without any restrictions. So from that point of view, it was quite a normal situation. I might just draw the following comparison: About a week ago I returned from Kabul. Kabul and such, it wasn't possible to move around there like that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of that period, did you witness any active discrimination against Albanians by any representative of Serbian authorities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DIETMAR HARTWIG
utterances.text: To be quite precise, I do not know anything of that, but I know an example. We lived in the house of a couple. The husband, I think, worked in the Serbian Ministry of Health, and his wife was professor at the university, and a daughter was a medical doctor, and today daughter was going through medical training. And he stated that they were -- they were fired due to the fact that they were Albanians. And then I asked the daughter on one occasions later on, and she said that the father went into retirement because of the age limit, and then -- so he gave up his -- and then the wife gave up her post because she wanted to join her husband. And the son said I had to treat a Serb patient in the hospital, and then I was made to leave. And I just gave this as one example. I'm not saying this was the principle in the whole of Kosovo. I always heard -- I don't know, I think there are 180 Albanians were fired, so they were unemployed. But nobody gave me an example in point which we could use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please stop here for today. Mr. Nice had some matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only very quickly. They are only very short. As to this witness and before he withdraws, in light of our interest and also the question asked by His Honour Judge Kwon about tab 1, it would always be open for the witness, since he has to come back, either to check his computer, or if indeed tab 1 was typed on a laptop, to bring his laptop with him so that we can see its generation date. Separately, I would ask that the witness search his records and/or his computer so that he can bring with us, if he chooses, the letter he sent to General Sreten Lukic on the 24th of March, I think it was of 2000. But in any event, he'll know the letter concerned. I have adequate secondary evidence of it, but it will save time if we simply have the typed copy of the letter that he sent to General Lukic. I regret that I do not have a file of materials to make available to the witness for him to pre-read for cross-examination, because I wasn't aware until he's given evidence, of materials that I might have wanted to research and free from restriction. So if things change, if, for example, I do find materials between now and the weekend, may I have leave of the Court, if the witness is willing, to present materials to him? But I don't think it's likely. But I suppose it would save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hartwig, you heard what the Prosecutor said. Those two pieces of material, if you have them, then bring them. Secondly, he may have material that you can pre-read, and which, if he does have, he would transmit to you over the weekend. Would you be in agreement with pre-reading that material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm prepared to read through the material, and I'm also prepared to look through my computer. It's a laptop which is 12 years old, and I know that in questioning General Lukic about a year or two years after my stay in Kosovo that I sent this to him, but I know that I did not store everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other two matters don't concern the witness but he doesn't need to withdraw. The first one, before we forget it, is that the video clip of Blace was adopted in part by the previous witness. I didn't ask for it be exhibited by oversight. May it be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are technical objections which, subject to anything Mr. Milosevic may want to raise himself I can raise them quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's deal with that at another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last point is this: Can I deal with this in private session for just one minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: With the witness present?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. I don't want to take time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender tab 2 into evidence. That is the presentation given at the conference in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That will be exhibited. We are adjourned until 9.00 a.m. next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
